program: Street-safety advocacy, research, organizing and crash-family support

what: Transportation Alternatives organizes for safer walking, cycling and transit across New York City.
This report includes its entire recipient, including Families for Safe Streets, research, membership and events.
Safer streets could avert serious injuries, but this review cannot establish the health return from an additional unrestricted gift.
strengths: Current campaigns organize around identifiable street-design decisions.
Original audits and tax reconciliations recover separately netted event costs.
The injury mechanism is more direct than assigning health value to petitions or cycling counts.
reservations: No evidence identifies how many additional corridor improvements an ordinary gift causes.
The DOT injury association is not a randomized estimate of future campaigns.
Public construction costs, travel changes and other portfolio effects may materially change total social value.

sections.what: Transportation Alternatives Inc., EIN 51-0186015, combines advocacy, organizing, research, membership and events. Families for Safe Streets is inside this recipient, not a second charity credited independently. Current work includes Central Harlem protected lanes, connected Brooklyn and Queens networks, speed-limit implementation and transit access. An ordinary gift supports this mixed portfolio, not a guaranteed lane project. [Current campaigns](https://transalt.org/citywide-campaigns) [Central Harlem proposal](https://transalt.org/citywide-campaigns/central-harlem-bikeway)
sections.monitoring:
Measure additional or accelerated implementation, collision risk and finite health, rather than campaign participation. NYC DOT's 2005–2018 evaluation reports an 18.1% before/after reduction in killed-or-severely-injured road users across 146 protected-bike-lane treatments and 36.7 centerline miles. Selection of dangerous corridors, regression to the mean and concurrent changes matter; the association is not a randomized causal contrast or an estimate of TA's contribution. A historical scenario halves the association, but this does not establish donation-driven implementation. The 31st Street proposal reports 26 people killed or severely injured during 2021–2025, giving 5.2 annual events as a selected high-risk corridor anchor, not a representative mean for TA's campaigns. [DOT evaluation](https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/downloads/pdf/safety-treatment-evaluation-2005-2018.pdf) [31st Street proposal](https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/pr2026/nyc-dot-redesign-of-31st-st-in-astoria-queens.shtml)

A useful recipient disclosure would list proposed, unsuccessful and implemented campaigns, prior city commitments, implementation dates, funding constraints and matched safety trends. Citywide improvements or income-group trends cannot identify TA's contribution. [DOT equity analysis](https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/pr2025/vision-zero-report-street-redesign.shtml)
sections.qualitative:
Protected street design has a plausible injury pathway, while public agencies retain legal, engineering and spending authority. Existing city projects, elected officials, other advocates and community demand remain in the counterfactual. Current Central Harlem organizing demonstrates an active opportunity, not a measured probability of success. The model represents four corridor-equivalent opportunities over an annual portfolio cycle, not four observed additional projects or credit for 31st Street itself.

The denominator includes only residents of the official 22-county New York–Newark–Jersey City MSA. A 95% resident share of the modeled injury benefit is an explicit judgment: city streets also serve tourists and commuters from outside this MSA. All five city boroughs are within scope; headquarters location alone is not the allocation method.
sections.cost:
The current cost per ten additional MSA-resident QALYs from an unrestricted gift is not established. Transportation Alternatives campaigns for safety improvements, but no source identifies how many additional corridor changes a gift causes, its share of a coalition's contribution, or the health effects of those changes.

The earlier $71.4 million per ten QALYs calculation remains below as a historical conditional diagnostic, not a measured central estimate or donor recommendation. It charged the full $5,186,682 annual recognized recipient expense to one street-injury pathway and assumed four corridor equivalents, 5.2 serious/fatal events per year from one selected street, 18.1% before/after injury association, 50% transfer, 25% incremental coalition effect, 30% TA share and 50% donation response. The implementation and attribution terms are not calibrated by those sources. Multiplying uncertain factors produces reproducible arithmetic, not a reliable unrestricted-gift estimate.

The historical exercise assigns finite health gains to avoided fatal and serious injuries, with explicit duration, utility and discounting choices; it does not value physical activity, air quality, accessibility, crash-family support, travel changes or harms. A separate illustrative public-cost case is not a construction quote. Zero implementation, donor substitution and adverse effects remain possible. A new central estimate would require a gift-responsive project pipeline, matched safety outcomes, defensible MSA residency and complete resource costs.
sections.funding:
March-ending audited expenses are $4,447,542 in FY2023, $5,135,283 in FY2024 and $5,186,682 in FY2025. Each reconciles to the original Form 990 expense plus separately netted fundraising costs of $67,853, $141,953 and $83,095 respectively. FY2024 expense includes a $206,481 employee-retention credit that reduced payroll-tax expense, so the three-year accounting mean is not an unadjusted recurring resource-cost baseline. No additional donated-service adjustment is reported in Schedule D; unrecognized volunteer opportunity costs remain outside this series. [FY2025 audit, Note 15](https://transalt.org/s/FY25-Transportation-Alternatives-Inc-Financial-Statement-FINAL-1.pdf) [FY2024/2023 audit](https://transalt.org/s/Transportation-Alternatives-Inc-24-AUD-FINAL.pdf)

FY2025 support and revenue were $4,335,312 and ending net assets $3,270,676, of which $523,106 were restricted. The unrestricted decline was $426,460; the full $851,370 decline is not an unrestricted cash need. The board designated $1 million as a stability reserve. Two donors supplied about one-quarter of FY2025 support and revenue. These facts support asking about funding resilience but do not identify gift additionality. The directory's displayed FY2025 period conflicts with the original audit: the report uses the year ended March 31, 2025, not March 2026. [Financial directory](https://transalt.org/financials) [Donation route](https://transalt.org/donate)

Expense appendix: FY2025 recognized costs comprise $4,317,855 program services, $371,200 management/general and $497,627 fundraising. The three-year recognized accounting mean is $4,923,169; reversing the one-off FY2024 payroll-tax credit for a sensitivity would make the mean $4,991,996, not change audited expense. Neither series includes all public or volunteer opportunity cost. Schedule D establishes the tax-return reconciliations.

model.costScope: Whole recipient annual recognized gross expense; one partial-health pathway, not full portfolio. Public implementation and unrecognized volunteers excluded except sensitivity.
model.geographicAttribution: Official 22-county MSA residents only; g=.95 subjective injury-beneficiary residency, not population share or five-borough geography substitution.
model.formula: Historical diagnostic only: A=sum(j=1..T)1.03^-j; D=u*(1-exp(-(ln(1.03)+m)*L))/(ln(1.03)+m); q=f*D+(1-f)*s; Qall=N*B*r*t*p*a*b*A*q-h; QNYC=g*Qall; price10=10*C/QNYC when positive. Current whole-recipient marginal health return is unidentified.
model.counterfactual: Existing city plans, appropriations, other coalitions and replacement donations continue. Only additional or accelerated corridor-equivalent years receive credit; no historical completion receives a new gift's credit.
model.attribution: p is incremental coalition effect, a TA's distinct share, b donation response. Each applied once. No independent credit to Families for Safe Streets or overlapping Open Plans work.
model.uncertainty: No current central unrestricted-gift estimate is established. Historical conditional partial-health scenarios contain uncalibrated implementation, attribution, funding and geographic choices; they are possibilities, not confidence bounds or a donor recommendation.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional corridor-equivalent years -> avoided fatal and nonfatal severe injuries -> finite discounted health.

sensitivity: Historical diagnostics only: implementation yield, causal share and gift response multiply; a zero in any one eliminates modeled benefit.
The favorable ten-year historical scenario yields about $1.1 million per ten MSA QALYs, not an upper confidence bound or current donor price.
Illustrative public construction costs raise the historical diagnostic; other transport benefits and harms remain unpriced.
